David visits Ahimelech (verses 1–9)

In distress, David fled to God's tabernacle.

It is a great comfort in trouble to have a God to whom we can go, explain our circumstances and ask confidently for guidance.

But David told Ahimelech a serious lie.

How should we regard this?

Scripture does not conceal it, and we must not defend it.

David did wrong, and the consequences were dreadful: his lie contributed to the killing of the Lord's priests.

Later, he remembered the deed with regret.

David had shown strong faith and courage before, but both failed him here.

Fear and weak trust led him into disgraceful wrongdoing.

Had he relied properly on God, he would not have resorted to such a sinful method to preserve himself.

The record is given as a warning, not permission to imitate him—even under the greatest pressure.

David asked Ahimelech for food and a sword.

The priest considered it lawful for David and his companions to eat the bread of the Presence.

Christ, the Son of David, later used this incident to teach that mercy takes precedence over sacrifice, and ceremonial restrictions must yield to moral duty.

Doeg entered the sanctuary just as David did.

We cannot tell merely by someone's attendance at public worship what is in that person's heart.

Some come sincerely to serve God.

Others pretend to worship while observing teachers and gathering accusations against them.

Only God, and later events, can distinguish David from Doeg when both are present in the tabernacle.

David pretends to be insane at Gath (verses 10–15)

Persecuted believers have sometimes been treated more kindly by Philistines than by Israelites.

David had reason to trust Achish.

Yet fear overcame him.

His behavior was humiliating and revealed that his courage and faith were wavering.

The more simply we trust and obey God, the more safely and peacefully we can make our way through this troubled world.

Verses 1-9
David, in distress, fled to the tabernacle of God. It is great comfort in a day of trouble, that we have a God to go to, to whom we may open our cases, and from whom we may ask and expect direction. David told Ahimelech a gross untruth. What shall we say to this? The Scripture does not conceal it, and we dare not justify it; it was ill done, and proved of bad consequence; for it occasioned the death of the priests of the Lord. David thought upon it afterward with regret. David had great faith and courage, yet both failed him; he fell thus foully through fear and cowardice, and owing to the weakness of his faith. Had he trusted God aright, he would not have used such a sorry, sinful shift for his own preservation. It is written, not for us to do the like, no, not in the greatest straits, but for our warning. David asked of Ahimelech bread and a sword. Ahimelech supposed they might eat the shew-bread. The Son of David taught from it, that mercy is to be preferred to sacrifice; that ritual observances must give way to moral duties. Doeg set his foot as far within the tabernacle as David did. We little know with what hearts people come to the house of God, nor what use they will make of pretended devotion. If many come in simplicity of heart to serve their God, others come to observe their teachers and to prove accusers. Only God and the event can distinguish between a David and a Doeg, when both are in the tabernacle. ( [1Sam.21.10-1Sam.21.15] 1Sa 21:10-15)
[1Sam.21.10-1Sam.21.15]
Verses 10-15
God's persecuted people have often found better usage from Philistines than from Israelites. David had reason to put confidence in Achish, yet he began to be afraid. His conduct was degrading, and discovered wavering in his faith and courage. The more simply we depend on God, and obey him, the more comfortably and surely we shall walk through this troublesome world.

David at Adullam (verses 1–5)

Consider how God can use people who seem weak and unsuitable to carry out his purposes.

The Son of David is ready to receive suffering people who willingly submit to his leadership.

He welcomes everyone who comes to him, however sinful and miserable they may be.

He transforms them into a holy people and employs them in his service.

Those who desire to reign with Christ must be willing first to suffer with him and for him.

Notice how tenderly David cared for his elderly parents.

His first concern was to find them a quiet, safe place to live, whatever might happen to himself.

Children should learn to honor their parents by caring for their comfort and well-being.

Even if they rise to positions of honor or become occupied with demanding work, they must not forget their aging parents.

The Lord directs the steps of a righteous person.

He will preserve his people for the work he has appointed, however hated and exposed they may be.

Saul orders the slaughter at Nob (verses 6–19)

Saul's conduct shows the cruelty of jealous malice and the miserable tricks it employs.

He considered everyone around him an enemy simply because they did not agree with everything he said.

Ahimelech answered Saul with the clear conscience of an innocent man.

But the evil spirit ruling Saul drove him to increasingly terrible wrongdoing.

He made accusations that were completely false and unproved.

Cruel rulers seldom lack instruments willing to carry out their cruelty.

After Doeg killed the priests, he went to Nob and killed the other inhabitants.

People whom God abandons to their own sinful desires can commit the vilest deeds.

Yet this judgment fulfilled the Lord's earlier warning concerning the house of Eli.

Saul acted wickedly, but God was righteous in permitting these events.

Not a single word of God's will and warning will fail.

Abiathar escapes and finds David (verses 20–23)

David mourned the calamity deeply.

It pains a good person to discover that something he did contributed to other people's suffering.

David must have felt particularly distressed because his earlier lie had helped bring about this terrible event.

He assured Abiathar that he would protect him and spoke confidently of his own preservation.

All who belong to the Son of David may be certain of finding refuge with him (Psalm 91:1).

Despite the disorder, danger and constant urgency of his circumstances, David still made time for fellowship with God and drew strength and comfort from it.

David rescues Keilah (verses 1–6)

When rulers persecute God's people, they should expect trouble from other directions as well.

A country is most likely to enjoy peace when it allows God's church to live in peace.

While Saul pursued David, the Philistines attacked Saul's country.

But David still regarded himself as a protector of the land.

Jesus Christ, our Savior, likewise acted for the good of those who mistreated him and left us an example.

Those who refuse to do good merely because their past service has not been rewarded are not following David.

God warns David to leave Keilah (verses 7–13)

David could rightly complain that his enemies repaid good with evil and love with hostility.

Christ was treated in the same shameful way.

David sought guidance from his great Protector.

As soon as the ephod was brought, he made use of it.

We possess the Scriptures.

Whenever we face a difficult choice, we should consult them: bring the Bible here.

David's prayer was both reverent and extremely specific.

God permits us to pray this way, explaining exactly which matter troubles us and asking for direction.

He knows not only what will happen, but also what would happen under circumstances that never take place.

Thus he knows how to deliver godly people from temptation and how to judge everyone according to their deeds.

Jonathan encourages David (verses 14–18)

David made no attempt to harm Saul.

He continued along God's path, waited for God's appointed time and was content to remain hidden in forests and wildernesses.

The world's cruelty toward some of its best people should lessen our love for it and increase our longing for the kingdom in which goodness and holiness will receive everlasting honor.

Jonathan came to comfort David.

As a godly friend, he directed David's attention to God, the foundation of all comfort.

As a self-denying friend, he rejoiced in David's approaching rise to the throne.

As a faithful friend, he renewed their covenant of friendship.

We should regularly renew our own covenant commitment to God and sustain our fellowship with him.

If a single conversation with a true friend can strengthen and comfort us, how much more can we expect from the continual support and powerful love of Jesus Christ—the covenant Friend of believers?

Saul is forced to abandon the pursuit (verses 19–29)

Even during his worst wrongdoing, Saul liked to speak as though he were deeply religious.

Such language, without corresponding actions, can deceive both the people hearing it and the people speaking it.

The mountain that separated Saul's forces from David became a picture of divine Providence standing between David and his destroyer.

Do not despair at the thought of problems yet to come.

Trust the Lord, whose counsel is wonderful and whose work is excellent.

Before he allows his promise to fail, he will use even an invasion by Philistines to bring about our escape—at the very moment when the danger appears greatest.

God requires complete dependence upon himself.

“If you do not believe, you will not be established” (Isaiah 7:9).

David refuses to kill Saul (verses 1–7)

God placed Saul within David's reach.

But this was an opportunity for David to demonstrate faith and patience.

God had promised David the kingdom.

He had not commanded David to kill the king.

David argued strongly against harming Saul, speaking both to himself and to the men accompanying him.

Sin is something that should alarm us.

We must resist every temptation toward it.

David was not satisfied merely with refusing to do wrong himself.

He also restrained the people around him from doing it.

By doing so, he repaid good for evil to the man who had repaid his good with evil.

All who call themselves Christians should follow this pattern: never be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

David explains his innocence (verses 8–15)

David had been falsely accused of seeking Saul's life.

He showed that God had given him the opportunity to harm Saul, but he refused to do so on principle.

He declared that he would never take private vengeance.

When people wrong us, we can trust the Lord to put matters right.

Even if justice does not come in this life, it will come at the judgment of the last day.

Saul is moved but remains unchanged (verses 16–22)

Saul seemed overwhelmed by David's kindness.

But many people grieve over their sins without truly repenting.

They weep bitterly yet remain attached to the very sins they mourn.

God fulfilled the promise David had trusted: he would bring David's righteousness into the light (Psalm 37:6).

People who carefully preserve a good conscience can entrust their reputation to God.

Sooner or later, he will make even hardened opponents recognize the people he loves.

Saul and David parted peacefully.

Yet Saul was convinced, not converted.

He was ashamed of his envy but still carried bitterness in his heart.

He was frustrated because, after finally finding David, he could not bring himself to kill him as planned.

Malice may appear dead while merely sleeping, and may later awaken with doubled strength.

Whether God protects us by restraining an enemy's hands or by changing that person's heart so that the enemy will not harm us, the deliverance comes from him.

It is evidence of his love and a pledge of his salvation, for which we should be grateful.

Saul speaks as quite overcome with David's kindness. Many mourn for their sins, who do not truly repent of them; weep bitterly for them, yet continue in love and in league with them. Now God made good to David that word on which he had caused him to hope, that he would bring forth his righteousness as the light, [Ps.37.6] Psa 37:6. Those who take care to keep a good conscience, may leave it to God to secure them the credit of it. Sooner or later, God will force even those who are of the synagogue of Satan to know and to own those whom he has loved. They parted in peace. Saul went home convinced, but not converted; ashamed of his envy to David, yet retaining in his breast that root of bitterness; vexed that when at last he had found David, he could not find in his heart to destroy him, as he had designed. Malice often seems dead when it is only asleep, and will revive with double force. Yet, whether the Lord bind men's hands, or affect their hearts, so that they do not hurt us, the deliverance is equally from him; it is an evidence of his love, and an earnest of our salvation, and should make us thankful.

Samuel dies (verse 1)

All Israel mourned Samuel, and with good reason.

He had prayed for the people every day.

People have hard hearts when they can bury faithful ministers without sorrow and fail to feel the loss of those who prayed for them and taught them the Lord's way.

Nabal refuses David's request (verses 2–11)

We might never have heard of Nabal if nothing had happened between him and David.

His name means “fool.”

Wealth makes people appear impressive in the world's eyes, but to someone who judges rightly, Nabal was a very small man.

He had no honor or honesty. He was rude, quarrelsome, ill-tempered, oppressive and willing to use fraud or violence to gain and preserve possessions.

What reason have we to admire worldly wealth when such a man can be rich while a good man such as David lacks necessities?

David pointed to the protection and kindness he had given Nabal's shepherds.

David's followers were themselves distressed, indebted and discontented, while supplies were scarce.

His careful leadership had kept them from taking what belonged to others.

But Nabal responded angrily to a request for help.

Greedy people often try to cover one sin with another, abusing the poor as a way of excusing their refusal to help them.

God is not deceived by that behavior.

We should learn to endure insults and false portrayals cheerfully and patiently, as many excellent believers have had to do.

Nabal insisted that the food on his table belonged to him.

But we are mistaken if we imagine that owning something gives us unlimited moral authority to use it however we please.

We are only stewards of possessions entrusted to us by their true Owner.

David plans revenge (verses 12–17)

God is kind even to the wicked and ungrateful. Why should we not act similarly?

David, however, decided to kill Nabal and everyone belonging to his household.

Could this really be David, who had spent so long suffering and should have learned patience?

Usually calm and thoughtful, he now became so enraged by a few offensive words that he was ready to destroy a whole family.

Even the best believers may show terrible corruption when God allows them to discover what is in their own hearts.

How urgently we need to pray: Lord, do not lead us into temptation.

Abigail brings a gift and speaks wisely (verses 18–31)

Abigail's gift made up for Nabal's refusal.

She approached David with great humility, speaking as someone asking for pardon.

A humble, yielding response can calm even a serious offense.

She could not defend her husband's conduct.

Rather than trusting the cleverness of her own arguments, she depended on God's grace to soften David's anger.

She reminded David that taking revenge on a weak and contemptible opponent like Nabal was beneath him.

Nabal would not do him good, but neither could he truly harm him.

God would preserve David and bring him through his present troubles to a glorious future.

It would therefore be wrong for David to take away anyone's life unjustly or unnecessarily, especially the lives of God's own people.

Abigail's strongest argument came last.

Refusing revenge would protect David's peace and conscience.

Many people have acted in fury and later regretted the decision a thousand times.

The sweetness of vengeance quickly becomes bitter.

Whenever we feel tempted to sin, we should ask how the action will appear to us afterward.

David is restrained; Nabal dies (verses 32–39)

David thanked God for sending someone to stop him before he committed a grievous sin.

Whenever we receive helpful counsel, encouragement, warning or timely correction, we should recognize God's kindness in sending it.

We should be thankful for providential events that prevent us from sinning.

Most people consider it enough to endure criticism patiently.

Few are grateful for correction or praise the person who gives it as a friend.

Yet the closer we have come to doing wrong, the greater the mercy of being stopped.

Sinners are often most confident of their safety when their danger is greatest.

Nabal, meanwhile, was drunk and felt completely secure.

He could not enjoy abundance with moderation or be pleasant with his companions without becoming beastlike through excess.

Nothing more surely reveals how little wisdom a person has—or destroys what wisdom remains—than habitual drunkenness.

The next morning his joy gave way to terror.

His heart, lively with wine the previous evening, became heavy as stone.

Such is the deception of fleshly pleasures: laughter quickly gives way to grief.

Those who drink to excess are saddened when they reflect on their own foolishness.

About ten days later, the Lord struck Nabal and he died.

David thanked God that he himself had been prevented from killing him.

Worldly disappointment, injured pride or a terrified conscience can end the pleasure of someone who lives for appetite and wealth.

But whatever instrument is used, death comes when God appoints it.

Editorially restored separate Concise exposition; absent from the pinned MHCC 0.1.1 compiled K body. See source provenance ledger.David marries Abigail (verses 39–44)

Abigail believed that David would become Israel's king.

She highly valued his godly and excellent character.

Although he was now in distress, she regarded his marriage proposal as an honor and a benefit.

She agreed humbly, in a way consistent with the customs of the time, and was willing to share his trials.

Verse 1
All Israel lamented Samuel, and they had reason. He prayed daily for them. Those have hard hearts, who can bury faithful ministers without grief; who do not feel their loss of those who have prayed for them, and taught them the way of the Lord.
[1Sam.25.2-1Sam.25.11]
Verses 2-11
We should not have heard of Nabal, if nothing had passed between him and David. Observe his name, Nabal, "A fool;" so it signifies. Riches make men look great in the eye of the world; but to one that takes right views, Nabal looked very mean. He had no honour or honesty; he was churlish, cross, and ill-humoured; evil in his doings, hard and oppressive; a man that cared not what fraud and violence he used in getting and saving. What little reason have we to value the wealth of this world, when so great a churl as Nabal abounds, and so good a man as David suffers want!, David pleaded the kindness Nabal's shepherds had received. Considering that David's men were in distress and debt, and discontented, and the scarcity of provisions, it was by good management that they were kept from plundering. Nabal went into a passion, as covetous men are apt to do, when asked for any thing, thinking thus to cover one sin with another; and, by abusing the poor, to excuse themselves from relieving them. But God will not thus be mocked. Let this help us to bear reproaches and misrepresentations with patience and cheerfulness, and make us easy under them; it has often been the lot of the excellent ones of the earth. Nabal insists much on the property he had in the provisions of his table. May he not do what he will with his own? We mistake, if we think we are absolute lords of what we have, and may do what we please with it. No; we are but stewards, and must use it as we are directed, remembering it is not our own, but His who intrusted us with it.
[1Sam.25.12-1Sam.25.17]
Verses 12-17
God is kind to the evil and unthankful, and why may not we be so? David determined to destroy Nabal, and all that belonged to him. Is this thy voice, O David? Has he been so long in the school of affliction, where he should have learned patience, and yet is so passionate? He at other times was calm and considerate, but is put into such a heat by a few hard words, that he seeks to destroy a whole family. What are the best of men, when God leaves them to themselves, that they may know what is in their hearts? What need to pray, Lord, lead us not into temptation!
[1Sam.25.18-1Sam.25.31]
Verses 18-31
By a present Abigail atoned for Nabal's denial of David's request. Her behaviour was very submissive. Yielding pacifies great offences. She puts herself in the place of a penitent, and of a petitioner. She could not excuse her husband's conduct. She depends not upon her own reasonings, but on God's grace, to soften David, and expects that grace would work powerfully. She says that it was below him to take vengeance on so weak and despicable an enemy as Nabal, who, as he would do him no kindness, so he could do him no hurt. She foretells the glorious end of David's present troubles. God will preserve thy life; therefore it becomes not thee unjustly and unnecessarily to take away the lives of any, especially of the people of thy God and Saviour. Abigail keeps this argument for the last, as very powerful with so good a man; that the less he indulged his passion, the more he consulted his peace and the repose of his own conscience. Many have done that in a heat, which they have a thousand times wished undone again. The sweetness of revenge is soon turned into bitterness. When tempted to sin, we should consider how it will appear when we think upon it afterwards.
[1Sam.25.32-1Sam.25.44]
Verses 32-39
David gives God thanks for sending him this happy check in a sinful way. Whoever meet us with counsel, direction, comfort, caution, or seasonable reproof, we must see God sending them. We ought to be very thankful for those happy providences which are the means of keeping us from sinning. Most people think it enough, if they take reproof patiently; but few will take it thankfully, and commend those who give it, and accept it as a favour. The nearer we are to committing sin, the greater is the mercy of a seasonable restraint. Sinners are often most secure when most in danger. He was very drunk. A sign he was Nabal, a fool, that could not use plenty without abusing it; who could not be pleasant with his friends without making a beast of himself. There is not a surer sign that a man has but little wisdom, nor a surer way to destroy the little he has, than drinking to excess. Next morning, how he is changed! His heart overnight merry with wine, next morning heavy as a stone; so deceitful are carnal pleasures, so soon passes the laughter of the fool; the end of that mirth is heaviness. Drunkards are sad, when they reflect upon their own folly. About ten days after, the Lord smote Nabal, that he died. David blessed God that he had been kept from killing Nabal. Worldly sorrow, mortified pride, and an affrighted conscience, sometimes end the joys of the sensualist, and separate the covetous man from his wealth; but, whatever the weapon, the Lord smites men with death when it pleases him.

David spares Saul again (verses 1–12)

How quickly an ungodly heart loses the good impressions once made by conviction!

Saul and all his men were completely helpless.

They might as well have been disarmed and chained, yet their only limitation was that God had put them into a deep sleep.

Achish trusts David; Saul becomes afraid (verses 1–6)

David faced a very difficult situation.

Refusing Achish's demand for military assistance would expose him to danger.

But if he promised help and then remained neutral—or turned against the Philistines—he would act ungratefully and betray their trust.

If he fought against Israel, he would sin gravely.

He seemed unable to escape without compromising his conscience.

Yet his ambiguous answer, intended to gain time, was not worthy of a true Israelite.

Trouble becomes terrifying to those who live in disobedience.

In his distress Saul inquired of the Lord.

But he did not approach in faith.

His divided heart made him unstable.

Saul had enforced the law against people who consulted familiar spirits (Exodus 22:18).

Some people appear zealous against wrongdoing only when they personally suffer from it.

They care little for God's honor and do not really hate sin because it is sin.

They condemn in others what they willingly practice themselves.

Saul tried to drive the devil from his kingdom while harboring envy and malice in his own heart.

How foolish to seek help from the very people he had tried to remove in obedience to God's law!

Saul consults the medium at Endor (verses 7–19)

Once we depart from the plain path of duty, nearly every choice leads us farther astray and increases confusion and temptation.

Saul asked the woman to summon someone from the dead.

God had expressly forbidden such practices (Deuteronomy 18:11).

Whether it is genuine occult activity or merely a pretended one, the attempt to obtain help or knowledge through a creature that cannot be obtained from God in the path of duty is either malicious or deeply ignorant.

While Samuel lived, Scripture never describes Saul consulting him in difficult decisions.

He should have sought that counsel then.

Now Samuel was dead, Saul asked for him to be brought back.

Some people despise and persecute godly ministers while they live and wish to have them back only after their deaths.

Henry concludes that this episode cannot be explained as a mere human trick or deception.

The woman had no power to summon Samuel by her own will.

But God may have permitted Samuel's appearance in response to Saul's inquiry.

The woman's surprise and terror show that what happened was unusual and unexpected.

Saul had rejected Samuel's solemn warnings during Samuel's lifetime.

Now he hoped, in defiance of God's command, to receive encouragement or advice from him.

God may instead have allowed the departed prophet to appear in order to confirm his earlier judgment and announce Saul's approaching death.

The words “You and your sons shall be with me” establish only that they would be in the world of the dead.

They do not establish the spiritual or eternal state of Saul or his sons.

The event solemnly shows God permitting a departed prophet to confirm from beyond the grave what he had already declared on earth.

Saul falls into despair (verses 20–25)

Anyone seeking help or comfort outside God's appointed ways will be disappointed as Saul was.

His terror led almost to despair, but not to humility.

He did not confess his sin.

He offered no sacrifices or prayers for pardon.

Nor does he appear to have considered the fate of his children and people or tried to escape the danger.

Instead, in stubborn despair, he moved toward destruction.

God has placed a few such examples in Scripture as warnings.

They teach us never to suppress conviction or despise the divine word.

But any sinner who still has even one thought of genuine repentance must not suppose himself beyond hope.

Let that person humble himself, seek the Lord's mercy and determine to continue seeking it throughout life.

Such a person will not seek God in vain.
